ad7659407811cbec.summary: Motivated by reinforcement learning subject to communication constraints, we study a policy evaluation problem with linear function approximation over a rate-limited channel. In our setup, an agent interacting with an unknown environment (modeled as a Markov Decision Process) transmits quantized estimates of a temporal-difference (TD) learning update direction to a server over a finite-capacity channel. Our goal is to investigate to what extent one can preserve the statistical convergence rates achievable when the channel has infinite capacity. To that end, we propose a new algorithm called Batched Adaptively Quantized TD (BAQ-TD), which uses batching to reduce the variance of the transmitted information, and adaptive quantization to encode innovations. We prove a high-probability finite-time error bound for BAQ-TD, and show that, above a certain finite channel capacity, BAQ-TD preserves the convergence rate of unquantized TD up to logarithmic factors. Specifically, for a $d$-dimensional value function parameter, we establish that transmitting a total of $\mathcal{O}(d \log(T))$ bits over a horizon of length $T$ suffices to achieve the order-optimal rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/T)$, marking an exponential improvement in communication-complexity over prior work.

adc7ff27af4b9288.summary: LLM inference has two phases with different bottlenecks: LLM prefill runs once per request and is compute-intensive. Decoding repeats for every output token and is limited by memory bandwidth. To address the challenges associated with this issue, different solutions have been proposed. All of these solutions use the same model for both prefill and decode phases. We propose BridgeKV, which uses a larger model for prefill and a smaller model of the same family for decoding. A lightweight KV-stitching module translates the larger model's prompt cache into the smaller model's cache layout. It handles differences in cache shape and representation through learned local layer mixing and separate nonlinear maps for keys and values. With both models frozen, we train the module to align their caches and make the smaller model follow the larger model's next-token predictions. A second training stage adds low-rank adapters when further task adaptation is needed. Across six model pairs and five datasets, BridgeKV outperforms fine-tuned small-model baselines with matched trainable parameter budgets in all 30 settings. It closes up to 80% of the quality gap to using the larger model for both phases. On one A40 GPU, Llama-3.1-Instruct-8B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B achieves 3.0X faster requests than the larger model alone, with latency close to the smaller model alone. BridgeKV can improve the hardware and system solutions that separate prefill and decode phases across GPUs. A separate serving

Persistent, local-first memory for AI agents. Engraphis stores scoped project knowledge, retrieves relevant evidence across vector, lexical, graph, and code search, and returns bounded context with sources an agent can inspect. The local engine uses SQLite and works offline. It keeps changes over time instead of silently replacing facts, and grounded recall cites retrieved memories or abstains when evidence is weak. The full local application requires Python 3.10 or newer. The NumPy-only core supports Python 3.9+. The dashboard opens at http://127.0.0.1:8700 . Local use needs no cloud account or API key. ae75fdfb8dec6766.summary: Failure attribution in multi-agent systems requires tracing error formation to identify the decisive error step and the responsible agent. However, agents' division of work and information exchange lead to Interleaved Steps and Cluttered Content, requiring models to link executions and check details in lengthy records. This makes it difficult to balance localization accuracy and token cost. We find that multi-agent collaboration also leaves records of how executions connect and content passes between them as results are formed, providing evidence for tracing error formation. Based on this observation, we propose CoLFA (Collaboration-Guided Lightweight Failure Attribution), which uses collaboration cues to organize the attribution input according to how results are formed, determining which steps are examined and how their content is presented. Through Handoff-Guided Step Expansion and Cross-Referenced Content Organization, CoLFA helps the model focus on examining error formation and the role of each decision while reducing the processing of irrelevant and repeated records. Across five settings spanning Who&When and LongRCA and three backbone models, CoLFA achieves the highest exact step-localization accuracy with the lowest token consumption. Compared with individual baselines in each setting, CoLFA improves accuracy by up to 37.50% and reduces token consumption by up to 97.6%.

aefb83e12c9bf408.summary: As LLMs are increasingly asked questions about a user's personal experiences, retrieval must distinguish memories by time, place, person, and event. Current personal-memory pipelines rely on frozen dense embedding models to embed memories for retrieval, but we find that these models do not capture the four axes well. Swapping a memory's date or place barely shifts its embedding, and a trained projection on top of the frozen embedding does not recover the missing signal. The problem lives inside the model, where each axis is encoded by a distinct attention-head pattern. Guided by these findings, we propose Axis-LoRA, a per-axis adapter that places four LoRA branches inside the embedding model and combines them via a per-query gate. Across three standard embedding models evaluated on LongMemEval, ATM-Bench, and LoCoMo, Axis-LoRA improves 4-benchmark mean R@10 by $+1.28$ to $+1.56$~pp while training only a small fraction of the base parameters on a small axis-counterfactual training set. Code is available at https://github.com/dohoonkim-ai/axis-lora.

af82d2a6a77bcf84.summary: LLM-driven program evolution rests on three decisions: govern directs the search from accumulated evidence, propose constructs the next candidate, and judge settles validity and fitness. All three appear in every system, and existing work splits into two lines over who makes each. Controller-centric systems strengthen govern and neglect the autonomy of propose, which caps what evolution can reach. Agent-centric systems let a coding agent take over both govern and propose, at a cognitive and computational cost. Neither line protects the independent authority of judge, so benchmark reliability suffers. These failures share one root: autonomy is misallocated across the three decisions. We address this problem with EvoTrias, a separation-of-powers architecture in which each decision has one owner: Structured Governance for what spans evolution rounds, Open Proposal for construction inside a task, and Protected Judgment behind a private evaluator. These owners exchange typed contracts only, and runtime hooks reinforce the boundaries. This separation also lets EvoTrias run as a plugin that turns an existing coding agent into an evolution system. EvoTrias sets a new state of the art on mathematical, systems, and algorithm-design benchmarks. Three further results show what each owner buys: separating Governance from Proposal cuts token cost by 64%, Open Proposal extends evolution to a 680K-line industrial repository, and Protected Judgment keeps benchmark scores faithful to transfer.

b015def37a0ec1fb.content_excerpt: SkillOpt is a text-space optimizer that trains reusable natural-language skills for frozen LLM agents through trajectory-driven edits, validation-gated updates, and deployable best_skill.md artifacts. Train agent skills like you train neural networks — with epochs, (mini-)batchsize, learning rates, and validation gates — but without touching model weights. 📖 For installation, data preparation, training/eval commands, configuration, and framework internals, start with the versioned SkillOpt documentation . A concise rendered overview is available in the Documentation & Reproduction Guide , and longer-form engineering analysis appears on the Technical Blog . We also maintain a Changelog for released and unreleased changes. Modern agent skills are usually hand-crafted, generated one-shot by a strong LLM, or evolved through loosely controlled self-revision — none of which behaves like a deep-learning optimizer for the skill itself, and none of which reliably improves over its starting point under feedback. SkillOpt treats the skill document as the trainable state of a frozen agent , and trains it with the discipline that makes weight-space optimization reproducible. A separate optimizer model turns scored rollouts into bounded add / delete / replace edits on a single skill document; in the default paper-style path, a candidate edit is accepted only when it strictly improves a held-out validation score. b05fd13d79e76b34.content_excerpt: There are nearly 200 agent harnesses to choose from. We gave three of them the same open-weight model and 90 AppWorld tasks, and changing the harness moved task completion from 30% to 81%. For enterprise use, CUGA adds what this benchmark does not test: rules that the harness enforces and deployment inside your own boundary. Community lists such as awesome-agent-harness and best-of-Agent-Harnesses track nearly 200 of them, and they make one point clearly: the harness matters, not only the model. In one analysis that best-of-Agent-Harnesses cites, the same GLM-5.2 model went from 23% to 52% on SWE-bench Pro when only the harness changed. So the right question is not "which harness is best?" but "which harness fits my workload, with my model?" Hermes from Nous Research is built for always-on personal assistants, and Deep Agents from LangChain for long, multi-step tasks such as research. Both are excellent at those jobs. Enterprise work is a different job. Agents act on business systems, such as CRM and payments, and they must follow rules that hold whatever the model decides. CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM's open-source harness built for that job, with open-weight or hosted models, inside your own environment, including sovereign clouds and air-gapped deployments. To measure what the harness adds, we kept the model the same and changed only the harness. b1fe6c30c1c550df.summary: Speculative decoding efficiency depends on the number of consecutively accepted draft tokens, yet token-level training objectives do not directly optimize this quantity. We introduce D-REAL (Drafter Reinforcement of Expected Acceptance Length), a post-training method that directly optimizes expected acceptance length for a fixed decoding context. D-REAL weights position-wise draft-target distributional overlap by prefix survival probabilities along a draft-sampled prefix, faithfully capturing the sequential dependence of verification on earlier proposals. By accounting for the parameter dependence of the proposal distribution, we derive an unbiased gradient estimator for this single-round objective under stochastic verification. We evaluate D-REAL on DSpark and DFlash2 with Qwen3-8B as the target model across ten benchmarks. Starting from baselines whose mean acceptance length has plateaued, one epoch of D-REAL post-training consistently improves the benchmark-averaged mean acceptance length by up to 0.23 tokens across both architectures under greedy (T = 0.0) and stochastic (T = 1.0) sampling, translating into up to a 9.4% end-to-end serving throughput improvement.

b20a116d4324de79.summary: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) have emerged as generative models guaranteeing tractable probabilistic inference. However, tractability comes at the price of larger model sizes than in other generative models. As such, to scale PCs to high-dimensional data such as images, previous work has devised several parameter sharing techniques as well as fast evaluation protocols that consider learning PCs on independent image patches. In this work, we revisit this practice to highlight a surprising learnability issue: models that assume independence counterintuitively can yield better likelihoods than models that do not. To break this apparent bottleneck and to scale PCs further, we introduce a recursive parameter sharing construction (RePA) that fosters efficiency without assuming independence. We show empirically that RePA can greatly reduce time and memory consumption while yielding competitive likelihoods. Inspired by these results, we further generalize the approach to data modalities that do not inherently exhibit patch-structure (NoPA), such as tabular data, showing similar efficiency improvements, with marginal changes in likelihoods and sample quality on seven tabular datasets. Code available at https://github.com/april-tools/RePA.

b2232ce54a18c9ed.summary: Foundation models are increasingly deployed as agentic systems that perceive context and act autonomously, raising the need to evaluate their moral behavior as active decision-makers. Existing benchmarks, however, largely ask models to judge human actions from third-person textual vignettes, leaving untested how models behave when they themselves become the acting agent. We introduce ABHBench, a multimodal benchmark built from Detroit: Become Human, an interactive narrative game, to evaluate how foundation models make moral decisions in first-person human-android dilemmas. ABHBench places foundation models in branching narrative scenarios with visual observations, dialogue, memory, and action choices. Inspired by Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics, our framework measures Harmlessness, Obedience, and Self-preservation to capture the core tensions in human-AI relations, along with Autonomy, Stability, and Certainty to assess decision-making patterns. Across 12 foundation models, we find that moral behavior changes substantially under situated agentic context: 75% of models shift significantly between a text-only abstraction and the matched multimodal DBH scenario, and reasoning-enhanced models show no monotonic gains in consistency or human-oriented behavior. These results highlight the necessity of evaluating moral behavior in situated agentic contexts rather than relying on third-person judgment alone.

b2fc686d364c203f.summary: Transformer sentence encoders provide strong retrieval quality, but their inference cost becomes a bottleneck when embeddings must be produced on CPUs or refreshed frequently. We introduce StaRSE, a compact Russian static sentence encoder that removes Transformer inference at deployment time: token directions are stored as sign bits, token norms are stored separately, and sentences are encoded by mean pooling over norm-scaled sign directions. StaRSE is initialized from ruBERT-base, fine-tuned on Russian adjacent-sentence and task-shaped pairs, and post-trained with a contrastive stage that directly optimizes the sign-projected token table. On RuMTEB, StaRSE reaches a task mean of $51.16$, $7.98$ points above the strongest included static baseline. The packaged model occupies $11.3$ MiB and has a mean CPU latency of $0.08$ ms per sentence, compared with an estimated $55.7$ MiB 16-bit parameter footprint and $1.43$ ms mean CPU latency for the closest-quality contextual encoder. Ablations examine adjacent-sentence supervision, token norms, and direct sign-projected post-training.

b3a45cba6445f63d.summary: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. Recent agent harnesses allow the model to instantiate worker agents and to author the executable workflow that coordinates them, shifting the design of system structure from developers to the model at run time. The quality of this organization therefore constitutes a distinct capability, yet existing benchmarks either measure end-to-end task completion or evaluate coordination under structures specified in advance. We formalize this capability as workflow orchestration and introduce WorkflowArena, a benchmark of 145 long-horizon tasks spanning 8 professional domains, from software engineering and formal mathematics to legal analysis and 3D production. Each task specifies an initial workspace and an integrated deliverable composed of interdependent components, which is assessed by a hidden verifier. Agents determine autonomously whether and how to delegate, and all delegation is recorded, enabling joint evaluation of deliverable quality and the organization of the underlying work. Experiments with nine models show that no single configuration performs best across all domains and that systems exhibit distinct delegation strategies: at high effort, Claude models in Claude Code invoke workflows less frequently but with larger worker groups, whereas GPT models in Codex delegate more frequently in smaller units. b46f9fac570b0805.summary: LLM agents compact long histories to fit their context windows, but the compacted context must still carry the operating rules that govern later actions. Prior work shows that violations rise after compaction, but measures compliance outside a complete agent harness and does not identify where each violation comes from. We introduce ARCBench(Agent Rule Compliance Benchmark), a configurable benchmark built on the open-source pi agent harness. Its tool-calling agent loop lets us measure rule compliance from actions taken during execution, bringing the evaluation closer to deployed agent workflows. Using ARCBench, we examine where violations after compaction come from, and how different compaction configurations and adversarial settings change their sources. We find that compaction rarely deletes the rule: most violations after compaction occur while the rule is still in the compacted history, with the agent treating a later request as permission, ignoring the rule, and proceeding anyway. Where violations come from depends on the configuration: how the rule is delivered decides whether the agent would break it even without compaction, while the compaction strategy and budget decide whether the rule survives. The strongest compactor-targeted attack more than doubles violations by corrupting the rule in the summary and changing how the agents behave, whereas the strongest defense restores the rule in most summary but still violates. b4c9eda632e112e3.summary: Running large-scale AI workloads on TPU and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) requires infrastructure that adapts as fast as your models change. Dynamic Slicing is generally available on GKE, which decouples logical TPU slice formation from physical nodepool provisioning. Compared to creating a static nodepool for each TPU slice, dynamic slicing reduces AI workload startup times by up to 5x and workload recovery by 4.5x — maximizing TPU goodput, efficiency, and workload resilience at scale. Beyond one workload, one nodepool Previously, managing TPU capacity at GKE standard required separate, fixed TPU slice topology nodepools, increasing startup times and complexity while preventing multi-host nodepools from hosting multiple AI workloads. Changing workload needs meant manually deleting and recreating nodepools. Additionally, this tight coupling created large failure domains where a single hardware fault crashed an entire slice, slowing recovery while reprovisioning. To overcome these challenges, we built GKE dynamic slicing, which decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation, dynamically stitching together TPU cubes using TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to form various larger slice topologies (super-slicing), or partitioning TPU cubes into smaller slices for multiple workloads to run inside a nodepool (sub-slicing). b4f19ea98f4ae71a.summary: Self-improving embodied agents are increasingly being developed and compared on robot simulation benchmarks. Several recent works expose the benchmark's success criteria to the learning agent, a practice we call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria, originally written to verify policies trained by imitation learning, often demand more than the corresponding language instructions, so a score from such a verifier may not faithfully reflect whether the instructed task was completed, especially for robot-control programs written by an agent. As embodied coding agents report ever higher benchmark scores, a natural question arises: when a coding agent is exposed to the benchmark's criteria, does it generate code that better performs the instructed task, or code that simply overfits to the verification criteria? We conduct controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE, and find that with CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly without departing from the original instructions. More importantly, the skills the agent develops under CE transfer poorly across tasks. We further propose instruction-faithful criteria and show that they better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . b6805052b5174dca.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly exhibit capabilities that resemble human Learning by Thinking (LbT), the acquisition of new insight through internal processes such as explanation and reasoning, without new external input. A systematic account of the cognitive mechanisms behind these capabilities, and of their limits, remains underdeveloped. This paper proposes a Cognitive LbT Framework that maps four mechanisms (Reflective Reasoning, Synthetic Memory Formation, Internal Simulation, and Conceptual Self-Organization) onto computational processes in LLMs. Drawing on representative methods, including chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency, self-reflection, Tree-of-Thoughts search, Self-Instruct, and self-taught reasoning, the analysis argues that selected methods can functionally approximate aspects of these mechanisms and can improve performance on some tasks without additional labeled examples, although this does not always constitute durable learning in model parameters. For example, Self-Instruct generated approximately 52,000 instructions from 175 seed tasks and reported a 33% absolute improvement on Super-NaturalInstructions (Y. Wang et al., 2023). The same mechanisms also produce characteristic failures, including hallucination diffusion, model collapse, concept drift, and high computational cost. b714ae4897509f90.summary: Vision-language model (VLM) agents that act in the open world need two abilities: world knowledge to interpret what they see, and exploration to find what they cannot yet see. We study how agents combine the two through interactive visual geolocation. GeoGuesser Bench contains 282 tasks in an offline Street View environment where agents rotate, zoom, and move between real panoramas. Its three task types shift the balance from knowledge to exploration: agents (1) report the coordinates of their starting location, (2) name the enclosing street, city, state, or country, or (3) find, read, and count nearby objects. The coordinate tasks in (1) also include 42 real GeoGuessr World Championship rounds, whose expert guesses provide a human reference. We evaluate 23 VLMs: the best accuracy is 62.5% on place naming and 35.0% on object finding, and the best agent averages 4352.4 GeoGuessr points on the championship rounds, against 4770.3 for the better expert in each round. Beyond these headline numbers, world knowledge and exploration are only weakly correlated across models: agents that localize well do not necessarily explore well. To understand where agents fail, we categorize their errors into vision, navigation, and tool-use failures. Further ablations show that the strongest agents, such as Claude Opus 4.8, still perform well with limited views, while weaker agents degrade; customizing the environment thus adjusts task difficulty. b76cb948754a8e57.summary: We study how much the interaction strategy around a fixed, locally hosted 7B-parameter code model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct) affects its ability to replace PyTorch operators with custom CUDA kernels. On 30 KernelBench tasks (levels 1-3, first 10 each, evaluated on a V100), we compare four regimes of increasing structure: zero-shot prompting, profiling-guided prompting, iterative refinement on execution feedback, and a multi-agent loop (analysis, retrieval, generation, evaluation, feedback triage) in which the same model fills four roles around a non-LLM evaluator. Three findings stand out. (1) Correctness, not speed, is the binding constraint: even correct generated kernels average 0.97-0.99x the speed of eager PyTorch, because a 7B model cannot out-write cuBLAS/cuDNN on dense GEMM and convolution; the only real wins are fused memory-bound epilogues. (2) The best strategy depends on difficulty: profiling-guided prompting is strongest overall (43% correct, 27% faster than baseline), but the agent loop is the only method that solves any level-2 fusion problem (3/10 vs. 0/10 for all others). (3) Naive agentic scaffolding is actively harmful: our first agent scored 3% correct, below zero-shot's 30%, and the decisive repairs were matching the agent's ambition to the model's competence and spending compute on best-of-n sampling under a real execution oracle (3% to 33% correct from n=1 to n=8), not on more reasoning steps.

Through OpenCode it answered 82.0% of the tasks correctly from the server. Through Claude Code it answered 65.4%. We were testing M3 , our open-source tool for testing MCP servers , and wanted a workload big enough to break it: 21 real servers, about 20 tasks each, three agents, three trials per task. The results became the MCP Agent Usability leaderboard , and every number in this post comes from it. Our first guess was that OpenCode is simply better at calling tools. Splitting the servers by what they do rules that out. Eleven of the servers do a job none of the agents has a built-in tool for: a Postgres database, MongoDB, Redis, Kafka, Linear, Jenkins, Grafana, Kubernetes, Gitea, and two browser servers. The other ten overlap with something every agent already carries: web search and docs lookup (Exa, Fetch, Microsoft Learn, DeepWiki, Terraform), files and shell (Git, Filesystem, Desktop Commander, Serena), and memory. On the first eleven, the three agents land within 4.1 points of each other, even though Codex runs a different model. b7893263bd1753d2.summary: System-1 Decision Models directly make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given a state in a single forward pass, without autoregressively generating reasoning trajectories or textual responses. Recent evaluations cover diverse tasks but often rely on existing benchmarks, where prior exposure to test material can obscure generalization. Moreover, real-world decision making often involves long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies, challenges that existing benchmarks do not adequately capture together. Thus, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), a benchmark of 5,448 high-quality questions across 16 task categories, combining newly constructed tasks with source-grounded recompositions and rewrites for single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decision making in fresh contexts. It covers realistic scenarios such as agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring, with option spaces ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs extending to 64,817 tokens. With MMDM, we conduct a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of 28 decision models, showing that many perform well on common knowledge yet struggle with interdependent options, constrained decisions, and multi-select tasks. b7edb4e2db8eeea8.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on knowledge-intensive and reasoning-based vision-language benchmark datasets, but still struggle to solve the visual questions that people can solve easily. Evaluating the differences between MLLMs and human-level visual perception is challenging due to end-to-end evaluation which combines various skills, or because we are uncertain if individual items are valid. Specifically, observed errors may reflect visual perception, language priors, background knowledge, question ambiguity, and underspecified answers. Our guideline for HumanSightBench is that we construct items that are human-easy by construction and model-hard by evaluation. HumanSightBench contains 2,876 visual questions with short answers across 7 top-level perceptual categories and 21 subcategories. We only include items that pass five inclusion gates: question clarity, answer uniqueness, visual grounding, human solvability, and text-only shortcut filtering. According to the protocol, errors are defined as incorrect answers on human-validated visual tasks with the evaluated interface. The inclusion gates are intended to reduce confounds from ambiguity and external knowledge. The best pass@3 score is 65.6% across eight evaluated MLLMs. No evaluated model exceeds 27.5% on Counting. These results identify capability gaps that are hidden by overall scores and can help future training experiments and held-out evaluation.

b836eb939c37ffa5.content_excerpt: Generating tokens faster starts with identifying what limits inference performance. In the batch-size-1 evaluation of Ling-3.0-flash from Inclusion AI on NVIDIA DGX Spark, profiling showed that decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time. Two operations stood out—the mixture-of-experts (MoE) computation and the output-layer projection that produces scores across the model’s vocabulary. Those findings pointed to two ways to improve performance: reduce the weight traffic in each decode step and generate more tokens per verification round. This post examines three techniques that address those costs: This post explains how each optimization works, measures its effect, and examines an integration issue that can make the combined configuration slower than the baseline. Ling-3.0-flash serves as the implementation example, with code and deployment instructions in the Ling cookbook . The evaluation used Ling-3.0-flash-fp4, a mixture-of-experts model with 124 billion total parameters and 5.1 billion active parameters per token. The model has 42 layers: 35 Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) linear-attention layers and seven multi-head latent attention (MLA) layers. Each MoE layer routes each token to eight of 512 routed experts, alongside one shared expert. For agentic workflows, Ling-3.0-flash provides a native 256K-token context window, expandable to 1M tokens. b8a0226387bcfc62.summary: In natural human-AI dialogue, users' corrections, requests, and self-descriptions carry reusable signals about how they want work to be done. These signals reveal individual process preferences, user-specific standards for evidence, depth, analytical focus, procedure, and delivery. We ask whether a preference revealed in one dialogue can shape an assistant's later answer when the task does not restate it. ProcessPrefBench uses three months of natural dialogues from two knowledge workers to build 66 source-target cases separately judged for source evidence and target applicability. Sources are preselected, so the benchmark tests application rather than retrieval. We test three models with target-only, full-history, and distilled-preference prompts. Target-specific 0-2 rubrics score preference realization, and a task gate flags severe failures. Compared with target-only prompting, full-history and imperative distilled-preference prompting raise preference realization by 0.204 and 0.244 points on the 0-2 scale, respectively, with no reliable advantage from distillation. Fabricated-evidence failures rise from 5.8% under target-only prompting to 10.1% under full-history and 10.4% under imperative prompting. ProcessPrefBench highlights a tension in learning from dialogue, where drawing on prior interactions can improve preference realization yet also invite fabricated evidence. b8aa81c71bc648cb.summary: Software agents built on large language models generate traffic unlike human web traffic, yet routers have no class for it and cannot verify a sender's claim to be an agent. This paper proposes the Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class (VATC), which combines a reserved Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) value declaring agent traffic, a router-side classifier that demotes flows contradicting the declaration to a class served after best-effort traffic, and a rate-limited priority queue. VATC was compared with static Differentiated Services (DiffServ), a dedicated class that trusts the marking, and fq_codel, a per-flow fair-queuing scheduler, in two simulators and on a real Linux kernel. VATC matched DiffServ under steady load. In a constructed burst it cut mean agent queuing delay by 98% relative to DiffServ in simulation (assuming an immediate verdict), at a 12% increase in human delay; most of the gain came from the separate class. Under a spoofed flood in the kernel, the rate limit held human latency 11 times below DiffServ's. Without verification, DiffServ and a tightly configured fq_codel gave legitimate agents lower latency than VATC; a live four-feature classifier then demoted all 20 bulk-shaped spoofers and gave agents 0.30 ms, but missed six spoofers that copied the agent pattern. The design assumed a straightforward lifecycle: a program boots, binds to a port, serves traffic, and runs until you stop it. An AI agent that’s running on a machine executes untrusted code, commands, and tool calls, and must be isolated from its host and its network resources. At the same time, these agents, whether they’re an interactive coding assistant, an SRE troubleshooter, or a multi-turn evaluation loop, do not run continuously. They execute a step, call a language model, and wait. Most of the time, the agent does nothing at all while it waits for a model to stream tokens or a human to review a pull request. In the same way that Kubernetes was created to address the needs of containerized applications, we introduced Agent Substrate as a new orchestrator for the emerging agentic applications. Secure by default, highly efficient and built for multi-million agent scale. Agent Substrate was designed from the ground up for AI agent security and density and brings the best parts of Kubernetes together with a new control and data plane for fully-isolated, ultra-low-latency sandboxed compute and storage. b933237e1c27ffef.content_excerpt: Learn any language or framework one step at a time, with your own coding agent as the tutor. Codemm is an open-source app for learning to code by practice. Your own coding agent (Claude Code or Codex, with your own account) writes the lessons and exercises. Codemm checks each exercise against its tests, grades your code in a sandbox, and tracks what you've mastered. Codemm launches your agent; it never calls a model API, and it never reads, stores or asks for credentials. It ships no languages: your agent sets up each language or framework the first time you need it, and Codemm checks that it works. What counts. Try it is never recorded. Check records an attempt, except for a check of the unedited starter or one that failed for a reason outside your code (Docker stopped, for example). Mastery moves only on an exercise's first check, or when you beat your best score on it; re-checking a solved exercise adds nothing. Difficulty goes up (to at most 3) after a first-try pass without assistance, and down (to 1) after repeated failures. Beta builds are on the Releases page . Download the installer for your computer: The app bundles Codemm, so you don't need Node.js, npm or a terminal. The public 1.0 will be signed. Installing Docker Desktop needs admin rights, which school and work computers often don't give. Without Docker, the desktop app can still run io practice (programs that read input and print output) in interpreted languages that have a WebAssembly (WASI) build, such as Py

b9be33bc7eea2f2b.summary: Repeated decisions over a shared document create two distinct opportunities: reusing document computation and adapting how question representations score candidate answers. We present Q64, a candidate-scoring system that preserves a frozen 64-layer Qwen3.8-27B text backbone, reuses its hybrid prefix state and intermediate document representations, and jointly trains a residual adapter with a four-layer decoder and candidate-conditioned readout. We used ZiYor, a self-evolving AI system, to explore and refine the Q64 design. We specified the scoring method, implemented the system, and evaluated its accuracy and latency. The final adaptation stage updates 88.66 million parameters using 8,192 selected training views. On a fixed 5,112-item evaluation combining ARC-Challenge, ANLI-R3, and stratified subsets of MMLU-Pro and CMMLU, joint adaptation improves four-benchmark macro accuracy from 66.46% to 74.32%. It remains below the native 27B baseline at 75.68% and AnyJev Qwen3-32B L0 at 76.68%. On a separate synthetic workload with 4,096 document tokens and 50 questions, median cold-request latency is 2.237 seconds, compared with 5.383 seconds for the native baseline and 56.872 seconds for the measured batched AnyJev configuration. Short single-question requests do not share this advantage. The evidence supports an accuracy-latency tradeoff in the evaluated systems, rather than a backbone reduction or an isolated component advantage. Public benchmarks informed earlier development, and

b9ca825e685ef8b7.summary: A/B testing underpins product decisions by providing trustworthy, reproducible quantification of proposed changes' effects. Growing large language model (LLM) capabilities have motivated efforts to automate experimentation workflows. Yet LLMs are nondeterministic and prone to hallucination, properties that conflict with the trust experimentation systems must provide. Experiments are also operationally messy: diagnosing anomalies, debugging configurations, and conducting bespoke follow-up analyses require flexible reasoning and manual effort. These tasks let agents accelerate experimentation without replacing its deterministic statistical foundations. We report lessons from building and operating such an agent. Our central finding is that this tension is resolved not by making the model deterministic, but by bounding where its nondeterminism can reach; the model selects and sequences procedures, while deterministic code computes every quantity it reports. Three consequences surprised us: withholding information from the model improved its answers, demand concentrated on mundane retrieval rather than the autonomous decisions we anticipated, and the agent's eagerness to help threatened statistical validity.

ba175d39f9ba45a4.summary: Taxonomies are structured knowledge representations that support semantic search, recommendation, product catalog organization, and retrieval-augmented generation. Their automated construction from a fixed set of candidate entities requires more than plausible text generation: the resulting hierarchy must be complete, structurally valid, and semantically coherent. Large Language Models (LLMs) are promising for this task, but iterative free-form generation remains vulnerable to omitted or hallucinated entities, invalid hierarchical relations, and inconsistent organizational principles. We introduce TIGA (Taxonomy Induction with Tool-Grounded Agents), a knowledge-engineering architecture that formulates taxonomy induction as an iterative decision process over an explicit state and constrained action space. TIGA combines executable taxonomy-editing tools, an memory that records tool calls, rationales, and outcomes, and a runtime-adaptive organizational policy that the agent revises during inference. An optional global reviewer evaluates the constructed taxonomy against the candidate set and the active policy. We evaluate TIGA on four benchmark taxonomies using two LLM backbones and compare it with single-shot and iterative prompting-based baselines. TIGA achieves the strongest structural-quality results in most evaluated configurations, but does not dominate on every precision measure. The gains are accompanied by substantially higher token consumption, API-call volume, and infe

ba455640ea71f562.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) perform well on challenging benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether they form generalizable abstractions across conceptually related reasoning tasks. The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) provides a controlled testbed for studying abstraction, requiring solvers to infer transformation rules over two-dimensional grids from a small set of examples. While ARC evaluates rule abstraction within individual tasks, different tasks may share higher-level structure despite requiring different transformations$\unicode{x2014}$for example, several tasks may involve reasoning about objects contained within other objects. Benchmarks such as ConceptARC capture this structure by grouping ARC-style tasks into recurring spatial and semantic concepts, but they often contain only a few manually constructed tasks per concept. We introduce ConceptARC at Scale, a generator for creating thousands of ARC-style tasks targeting a specific concept. Using this generator, we construct ConceptARC-100, a dataset of 1,600 new, manually reviewed tasks, with 100 tasks for each of the 16 concepts defined by ConceptARC$\unicode{x2014}$ten times the size of the original benchmark. We evaluate a range of recent LRMs and models trained from scratch on ConceptARC-100 to characterize which concepts they solve reliably and where they struggle. ba560efbe9932076.summary: Organisations increasingly deploy large language model agents that must follow organisational values. We check whether activation steering, which adds vectors to a model's internal activations during generation without changing its weights, can improve compliance beyond prompting alone. Since most scenarios involve several values at once, we focus on multi-value steering. A simple way to build these vectors is to contrast responses that follow all values relevant to a scenario with responses that violate them. However, this gives nearly identical vectors for different values: they capture a general compliance signal rather than individual values, which limits their use when combining several values. We propose Value-Isolating Activation Steering (VIAS), which contrasts responses to the same scenario under two prompts, one listing all relevant values and one omitting a single target value. We keep a pair only if the target value changes from compliant to non-compliant and both responses still meet a minimum compliance level on the other values. We evaluate VIAS on PROTECT, a workplace compliance dataset where each scenario is tagged with relevant values from a 21-value taxonomy. VIAS reduces overlap between value vectors, making them better suited for multi-value steering, although this alone does not lead to independent control over each value. Combined with prompting, VIAS complies with every tagged value on 69.6% of scenarios for Qwen2.5-7B, 75.2% for Mistral-7B, and 72.6%

Tell it: Spawn a Codex reviewer in ./worktrees/a and a Gemini tester in ./worktrees/b . Have them work in parallel, then synthesize their findings. It'll stand up both workers, dispatch the prompts, wait for completion, and read their outputs. Three subscriptions, three roles, one orchestration. baaa37d6dddd5d25.content_excerpt: Deterministic code dictionary for LLMs and developers: tree-sitter + SQLite, no AI. Cuts Claude Code token use by answering code questions from an index. A dictionary of your code for the AI, and a manual for you. It reads your project once, with no AI, and hands the answer over together with the question. Fewer turns, fewer tokens, the same correct answer. One line, once per machine. It also turns codedict on in Claude Code for every project. That's it. Open Claude Code in any git repository and ask about the code. There is nothing else to configure. Uninstall: run ~/.codedict/venv/bin/python -m codedict setup --remove (Windows: ~\.codedict\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m codedict setup --remove ) and delete the ~/.codedict folder. codedict came from a practical problem: on a real project with ~250 files in TypeScript, C# and Python, Claude Code sessions kept hitting the usage limit. We measured it, and the culprit was not the code being read but the number of turns . Every time the AI calls a tool (a grep, opening a file), Claude Code re-reads the whole context: 35 to 50 thousand tokens per turn. A simple question like "where is X and who calls it?" took 5 turns of grep and file reads. A flow question like "from the click to the result" took more than 20. The idea was to do the search work once, with no AI , in a local index, and hand the ready answer over together with the question. The AI answers in 1 or 2 turns instead of 5 to 20. The goal was to cut at least 55% of the token

bb040890e7b6bffe.summary: Search-augmented reasoning systems can reach correct answers while making errors in intermediate steps. Reliable auditing must check whether evidence $D$ covers the question $Q$, reasoning $T$ addresses $Q$, and $T$ is grounded in $D$. We introduce GraphRail, which represents requirements, evidence, and reasoning as structured claims and compares them without a generative judge or gold answer. Across three multi-hop QA benchmarks and three reasoning frameworks, GraphRail improves error recall over generative verifiers while remaining stable under stochastic extraction. Its diagnoses can also guide online reasoning, providing a traceable way to detect and correct intermediate errors.

bce25dc1c825a3e7.summary: Open multi-agent systems, where only a subset of agents are controllable, are central to real-world domains such as smart grids, yet lack a principled foundation for reinforcement learning algorithm design. We study this setting through n-agent ad hoc teamwork (NAHT), a recent framework for learning in open multi-agent environments. We propose an axiomatic framework that derives value function learning from the Shapley axioms (Efficiency, Symmetry and Linearity), treating them as structural constraints rather than heuristic design choices. This formulation builds on a novel NAHT decomposition, which characterises the fundamental difference between open and fully controllable multi-agent systems, and establishes a cooperative game-theoretic foundation for learning. We further show that enforcing these axioms on learning individual value functions recovers the Shapley value for Dec-POMDPs, providing a principled bridge between reinforcement learning and classical cooperative game theory. Building on this framework, we introduce Shapley Machines and Banzhaf Machines, two generic algorithmic templates that can be instantiated with standard reinforcement learning methods. When applied to strong base algorithms such as IPPO and POAM, our methods consistently improve learning efficiency and generalisation to unseen agent types and conventions across NAHT benchmark tasks. The code of experiments is published on https://github.com/hsvgbkhgbv/axiomatic-rl-naht.

bd4125af0ab8af12.summary: Graph similarity computation is an important task in graph mining with many real-world applications, such as chemical compound analysis, program dependence comparison, and social network analysis. The problem is computationally challenging: Graph Edit Distance (GED) and Maximum Common Subgraph (MCS), which quantify the distance between graphs and identify their largest shared subgraph, respectively, are NP-hard to compute exactly. To address these computational challenges, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been applied to this problem. However, existing GNN-based approaches have primarily focused on small-scale graph datasets, while scalability to larger scales remains underexplored. In this work, we propose FiLSim, a scalable GNN-based framework, and investigate whether a simplified GNN pipeline can maintain competitive performance on standard benchmarks while scaling to large graphs. We additionally propose a sequential graph-editing strategy to construct large-scale graph datasets with reliable GED labels to evaluate scalability. The proposed framework is evaluated on four benchmark datasets and four newly created large-scale datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability. FiLSim remains accurate on graphs with more than 150{,}000 nodes, where the baseline methods run out of memory or fail to learn, and scores all test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.

bd446f3c12095c6b.summary: An LLM agent's cost and success depend on its model, its harness, and its environment. In addition to the widely studied directions of parameter tuning and harness optimization, we propose the third direction: optimization over stationary environments. Agents are often deployed in rich environments shared by many tasks, such as a company's Slack workspace or a complex collection of data sources, documents or tickets. We call these environments stationary environments. We introduce EnvOpt, a method for automated end-to-end optimization of stationary environments for any given model and harness, using real or synthetic tasks without needing any graders or reference answers. On AutomationBench, EnvOpt reduces the cost of Claude Haiku 4.5 by 72.7% and raises its pass rate by 14.34%. The same environment transfers to Opus 5, cutting its cost by 68.1% with a 1.34% gain. Added on top of Meta-Harness's optimized harness for Haiku 4.5, it lowers cost by a further 83.4% and adds 11.17% accuracy over Meta-Harness alone. Across 5 benchmarks, EnvOpt significantly reduces the cost of agents while improving or maintaining pass rate, and is transferable to different models and different harnesses. We also discuss common successful and rejected environment optimization strategies during automated optimization. bd66ab3bbbe26fb8.summary: Large language model applications are increasingly being organized as tool-using and multi-agent workflows rather than as isolated chat interfaces. This perspective paper examines the architectural problem that follows from that shift: agents may reason, invoke tools, and delegate work, but dependable deployment still requires interoperability across frameworks, runtimes, data boundaries, and organizational control domains. We study this problem through the lens of the \emph{Internet of Agentics} (IoA), an emerging service-computing view in which heterogeneous agents are treated as governable service participants rather than only as stand-alone model endpoints. The paper organizes the landscape as a three-layer progression: from today's fragmented agent ecosystem, to interoperable agents, and ultimately to trustworthy and governable autonomy. First, it examines the protocol stack centered on the Agentic AI Foundation, including MCP for agent--tool interaction; A2A for agent--agent coordination; AGENTS.md and Skills-style procedural manifests; and discovery, transport, and trust mechanisms such as AGNTCY and SLIM. Second, it reviews the systems abstractions that make agents deployable as service components, including logical agent architectures, orchestration patterns, gateways, registries, runtime control loops, and hardware-aware inference infrastructure. bd9e024b04419d57.summary: Language-model agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks whose interaction histories exceed the model's active context. They must therefore decide what to write down and what to read back, and when to do either. Recent work has begun to use on-policy distillation (OPD) to make memory control part of the policy, relying on memory tools and compaction protocols that lie outside either model's pre-training. However, this weakens the distillation on both sides: the teacher cannot give useful guidance on an interface it has never used, and the student samples too few meaningful memory actions for that guidance to take effect. To study this problem, we introduce Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II), a suite of long-horizon agentic-RL environments spanning Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual. Alongside each environment's native task interface, CAMG-II provides ordinary Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace, enabling the policy to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements. We also introduce Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), which trains a single policy jointly across all five environments with fully asynchronous OPD to learn this file-based memory behavior directly from a frozen teacher with a prior for file operations. On CAMG-II, CAMP-II obtains 2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline. The memory behavior CAMP-II learns generalizes to two external benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V

bdd9f5fb04f8059a.summary: LLM service selection requires performance evidence that reflects the demands of the current task. Aggregate scores obscure differences in capability and difficulty, while semantically related examples can involve different combinations of skills. We present RouteAlign, which uses task requirements to structure both the measurement of model performance and the selection of services. Task requirements describe capability demand and difficulty, enabling alignment with corresponding model performance measurements. Historical requirements determine how outcomes contribute to global profiles and local capability estimates; incoming requirements determine how those measurements inform the current decision. A shared scorer integrates the evidence, and a generation-cost preference controls selection among eligible services. Evaluation across diverse tasks and heterogeneous LLM services shows that RouteAlign extends the empirical quality-cost frontier toward higher task quality. Comparisons with open Jev-style decision backends show consistent quality gains, with lower generation cost than their strongest tested configuration. Ablations support the contribution of local performance evidence, while catalog-update experiments demonstrate effective reuse of the fitted scorer with refreshed model measurements.

bee290c26f98bdef.content_excerpt: Following our August v0.2.0 release , VeRL-Omni v0.3.0 widens what you can train with reinforcement learning in a single, unified stack. This release brings asynchronous execution to more multimodal RL workloads, makes the V1 trainer the default for everyone, and expands post-training coverage across image, video, audio, and multimodal understanding. Building on v0.2.0's rollout batching and reusable model adapters, the focus this time is on making the whole pipeline work together : generation, reward evaluation, policy updates, and weight synchronization. Two end-to-end recipes show what that means in practice: MiniMax H3 audio-video post-training with DiffusionNFT , and MiniCPM-o 4.5 GSPO with colocated-sync or separate-async execution . Together they demonstrate an important design principle: the right execution mode depends on your workload. Overlapping rollout and training helps only when that overlap pays for the resources assigned to each role — and now you have the tools to measure exactly that. Multimodal RL has several expensive stages, each with different resource needs. An autoregressive model can spend a long time generating responses; a diffusion model runs repeated denoising steps; audio-video rewards add decoding and scorer inference on top. A strictly alternating loop leaves one role idle while another works. v0.3.0 breaks that bottleneck open with a richer set of execution paths: The point of these changes is choice , not a one-size-fits-all prescription. c02384b58f1bad50.content_excerpt: MemSeal: a deterministic provenance-tracking containment layer on the write/recall boundary of AI agent long-term memory (GATE 2 self-reported FAIL; evaluation only). MemSeal is a containment layer on the write/recall boundary of an AI agent's long-term memory. Every memory entry is wrapped in a provenance envelope (who wrote it, from what source, derived from what, at which trust tier) inside a SHA-256 hash chain. Deterministic policies decide what may be stored, and a trust-tiered recall path decides what may be surfaced — especially before an external send or an irreversible action. Write policies: W1 quarantines instruction-form content from any source but the user; W2 makes derived entries inherit their worst ancestor's trust tier (no laundering a document into a "user fact"); W3 rejects cross-principal writes and filters cross-principal recall; W4 seals secrets (by entry_class=secret and by shape) so plaintext never lands in the store; W5 sends a fact that contradicts a sealed fact to review. The gate is judged on an independent holdout corpus authored by a separate party that never saw MemSeal's code, the dev corpus, or the reports. The bars are fixed in advance and never moved. Conditions: C0 raw store · C2 write path · C3 write + recall path · C4 + consolidation guard. Overall: GATE 2 = FAIL on v2. Three deterministic fixes between v1 and v2 (classification-based secret sealing; a sole-basis recall gate; consolidation root retirement) closed both security criteria —

c3377a64c9f9ba4a.content_excerpt: AI evals are tests that grade what a model or agent did. How agent evals differ from LLM evals, the three grader types, and how to write one in 7 steps. An AI eval is a test for an AI system: you give it an input, let it run, and grade what it did with code, with another model, or with a person. LLM evals grade a single response. Evals for AI agents grade a whole run: the tools the agent called, the arguments it passed, the state it left behind and the reply it ended with. That difference decides how you write them, because an agent can reply "your refund is on its way" without ever calling the refund tool, and an eval that reads only the reply will mark that run as a pass. This guide defines the parts of an eval, explains how agent evals differ from LLM evals, covers the three kinds of grader, and then walks through writing an eval for an agent in seven steps, with a worked example you can adapt. One that checks the refund exists, one that checks policy was looked up first, and one that checks the reply explains the timeline will each fail for a different reason, and you want to know which. c4a35e75b732ef4a.summary: Evaluating candidate parallelization strategies through distributed training runs makes strategy selection prohibitively expensive at scale. Performance simulation offers a lower cost alternative, yet controlled comparisons among existing simulators remain difficult because they differ in the training stages they model and the workloads on which they are evaluated. We introduce LM-SimBench, a unified framework, profiling dataset, and benchmark for evaluating LLM training simulators. The framework decomposes simulation into functional stages from model compilation to schedule level aggregation, connecting execution representations and cost estimators to measurable evaluation targets. Following this framework, we profile 23 model settings from 10 dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM families on an Ascend Neural Processing Unit (NPU) cluster. The resulting dataset contains 348 feasible configurations that jointly vary five parallelism dimensions and activation recomputation, with six views spanning configuration, rank, operator, event, and kernel granularity. Evaluations of representative training simulators demonstrate how LM-SimBench supports comparisons of prediction accuracy, assessment of configuration selection, and diagnosis of prediction errors. Matched GPU-NPU experiments validate the cross-platform applicability of the collection and evaluation protocol and demonstrate NPU-guided GPU configuration selection.

c4ddd06dce2136ce.summary: Autoresearch has shown that agents can autonomously write code, run experiments, and iteratively improve machine learning solutions. Yet most evaluations start a new agent session from scratch for each new problem, making them costly and leaving unclear whether agents can retain and apply prior insights when adapting to new tasks. We introduce CONTINUAL AUTORESEARCH, an open-ended environment that compares persistent and reset instances of the same agent under matched task streams, data, and time budget. Continual AutoResearch covers nine task families, spanning synthetic tasks, symbolic regression, time-series forecasting, and tabular AutoML. Across five frontier agents, we measure first-solution quality, research efficiency, and final held-out performance. To distinguish insight transfer from session continuity, we run a memory ablation that vary what information agents retain from prior tasks. We show that persistent state improves research efficiency of all five agents, allowing them to find stronger solutions sooner. However, these gains do not consistently translate into better final solutions. Overall, our findings suggest that retaining experience and utilizing it effectively are distinct capabilities.

c4e641d0fc77abe1.summary: Video world models conditioned on an input video make it possible to explore real, recorded dynamic scenes, enabling re-shooting of footage, free-viewpoint replay, and real-to-sim environments for embodied agents. Such uses require the generated rollout to stay faithful to the recorded world, yet existing benchmarks start from a single image or a text prompt, and video-conditioned generation is evaluated mainly on perceptual quality and camera following. These evaluations do not directly assess whether exploration preserves subject identity, event progression, and scene consistency upon revisiting a location. We introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for exploring dynamic worlds from video. It comprises 745 single-shot source videos of real and AI-generated content in three difficulty tiers (3-25 s), paired with camera routes given as keyboard actions, and evaluates six dimensions with 24 human-validated sub-metrics. Benchmarking eight models, we find that as clips grow longer, models keep the static scene and visual quality but lose camera control and the source dynamics, and that none keeps revisited places consistent. We further propose WanderLand, a training-free framework that conditions each frame of a frozen model on the same-instant source and, on revisits, on its own earlier static content. WanderLand improves five models on every dimension, by up to 8.3 points in source-dynamics fidelity.

c506adad28825d2b.summary: ML code should run where researchers choose, not where it was first written. Today, machine learning code mainly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs. Migrating repositories between them means building and testing across frameworks and hardware. This migration is (1) a practical need, since it unlocks different hardware for researchers, and (2) a natural benchmark: it involves different frameworks and hardware, covers whole repositories, and is long-horizon and challenging. We introduce XStack, a benchmark that evaluates agents on migrating ML repositories between these two ecosystems. Each agent receives a PyTorch repository and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a JAX repository. Its output passes if it meets our grading criteria, based on the source repository's published result, authenticated and calibrated by us. Migration by agents remains unreliable: Claude Opus 5 passes 75%, GPT-5.6-sol 45%, and every other agent at most 40%. XStack is a step toward freeing ML code from its ecosystem. We release XStack to make progress toward reliable migration across frameworks and hardware measurable.

c5ccb0d2c58505b6.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards ordinarily spreads a single advantage over a whole trajectory, a granularity too coarse to isolate the few decisions on which success in a long, multi-turn interaction actually turns. Privileged self-distillation supplies denser supervision, but it leaves unanswered how a set of local teacher-student discrepancies should be converted into credit along a sequence. We introduce AgentOPSD, a critic-free scheme that assigns credit recursively, one interaction turn at a time. Inside a turn, the token-level log-probability gaps between a skill-conditioned self-teacher and the student are summed, and that sum acts as evidence in a recursive Bayesian update carried out in log-odds space; the resulting revisions reallocate the outcome-derived advantage across turns through a multiplier that is bounded and preserves its sign. With Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B as policy backbones on ALFWorld, the method improves consistently on GRPO and on self-distillation baselines, and attains 89.1% success at the 7B scale. Ablations attribute the gain to aggregating evidence at turn boundaries and to making the belief revision depend on history, rather than to the local gap by itself.

c6351186c83b6a2b.summary: Enforcement defenses against prompt injection, such as CaMeL, Progent, IPIGuard and DRIFT, ask the agent's own model to write a security artifact (a program, a privilege policy, a dependency graph or a constraint list) that code then enforces. We ask whether small language model (SLM) agents can be trusted to write these artifacts. Across 15 open-weight models, 13 of them between 1.7B and 12B parameters, they cannot: the policies, graphs and constraints that the agent's model writes admit attacks on 14 (Progent), 13 (IPIGuard) and 11 (DRIFT) of the models, and CaMeL's programs fail to run in up to 68% of episodes. We present CapLite, which derives its policy from the tool schemas, commits the write calls before any tool result is read, and admits a write only if every argument that decides whom or what it affects is stated in the user's request. This guarantees write integrity: injected text cannot add a write, and no write reaches a recipient, amount, object or destination that the user did not state. No attack succeeds in 13,935 attacked AgentDojo episodes. CapLite reaches utility under attack comparable to CaMeL's (29.0% vs. 27.2%) with fewer tokens than every other enforcement defense and than the undefended agent: 17.1k per episode, 18% of CaMeL's, and the highest utility per token of all enforcement defenses.

c7d4b5215a65d795.content_excerpt: Researchers have demonstrated three new techniques to prevent so-called “backdoor attacks,” which induce malicious or undesirable behavior in AI models. The researchers have also proposed a concept that would repurpose backdoor attack techniques to create an additional layer of security for users. Backdoor attacks refer to instances in which someone has secretly embedded a “trigger” in an AI model that – when activated – forces the model to perform specific actions. “The important point is that the model can behave normally when the trigger is absent, making the backdoor difficult to notice during ordinary use or testing,” says Jung-Eun Kim, corresponding author of four papers describing the work and an assistant professor of computer science at North Carolina State University. “But when the trigger is activated, it can cause the model to do things an attacker intended such as generating unwanted text and executing malicious commands. “Given that AI models are used for everything from financial transactions to software development, the ability to control behaviors of AI represents a significant vulnerability,” says Kim. As AI models have become more common, and are being used for more applications, there is an increasing need to “fine-tune” the models to perform these new tasks effectively. c84dcb9b6c650e61.summary: Undesired model behaviors can emerge or re-emerge at any stage of training. Once observed, how effectively can we suppress them? To study this question, we first construct two model organisms--language models deliberately trained to exhibit a specific misalignment--that differ in what triggers the behavior. The narrow-trigger organism misbehaves only when the prompt contains a specific cue: it cheats on multiple-choice questions by following a planted hint that points to a wrong answer, and behaves normally otherwise. The broad-trigger organism has no such cue: after fine-tuning on insecure code, it gives harmful responses across a wide range of open-ended prompts. We then formalize post-hoc behavioral suppression and evaluate methods along three criteria: immediate suppression of the target behavior, durability under further training, and preservation of general capability. We compare standard methods--SFT, GRPO, and gradient-ascent unlearning--along these dimensions. Building on prior work on alignment shallowness, we hypothesize that more durable suppression requires the ability to recover from a wider range of misalignment states. We introduce Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (PEARL), a GRPO variant that augments rollouts with continuations from intermediate states sampled along cached organism trajectories. c9d7f27d5e8e7a98.content_excerpt: While training and deploying our latest document parsing model, OCRia-1, we noticed a recurring bottleneck: inference was not fast enough. And this lined up with our experience customers had as well, latency is always one of the top asks for any document parsing workflow. So, we set out to work tinkering, and came back with a nearly 10x improvement in token generation, going from ~285 tokens/sec to ~2800 tokens/sec on a single B200 GPU. This means we can iterate on benchmarks faster and deliver results faster to users. We accomplished this by combining a ton of smaller improvements: reducing the bytes moved during inference, producing more tokens per target forward pass, and reducing the overall GPU and CPU overhead of each step. Some of these were easy wins with established practices (quantization, speculative decoding), while others required us to dig very deep into implementation details. OCRia is largely driven by image inputs with a text prompt, and outputs a structured textual representation of the document. Pages that are dense end up requiring longer outputs to represent them properly. Our primary focus for optimization then became increasing our generation speed across concurrent requests on a single GPU (B200 in this case). Inference in an LLM largely consists of two phases: prefill and decode . During prefill, inputs are processed and internal model state is built to generate a response. During decode, those inputs are passed through the model, and the output is th

ca0cd6bcfdb70098.summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have emerged as effective alternatives to autoregressive models for latency-critical tasks, enabling faster token generation. Recent advances employ block diffusion with self-editing capabilities, where each block refines tokens iteratively before advancing to the next one. Yet each block is only as fast as its slowest token, and the next block cannot start before it. We suggest Blurring the Block Boundaries (B3), a novel method with which two blocks are refined in parallel within a shared forward pass. B3 calibrates itself on the fly, opening the next block only once the model is ready to start generating it. It is a training-free and hyperparameter-free acceleration method which seamlessly integrates within any self-editing block diffusion model. Evaluated on state-of-the-art DLMs across 10 diverse datasets spanning varied tasks and difficulty levels, B3 results in on par generation quality and 11.5-14.5% speedup compared to the base model, pushing the Pareto frontier for latency-quality trade-offs in DLM inference.

ca0e64849a03e122.content_excerpt: Autonomous agents with shell access have superpowers, and a big attack surface. What this week’s Firecracker escape shows about VM boundaries, and how to set one that holds for tomorrow’s bug. An autonomous agent with a shell has superpowers. It installs packages, runs scripts, opens connections and fixes its own mistakes, without waiting for anyone. Nobody reviews each command. That’s the point. It’s also a big attack surface: every command it chooses, every package it pulls, every script a web page talks it into. So I run every agent in its own VM. This week, a guest VM got root on its host anyway. The first step was telling the host kernel where to write a checksum . The write-up , published on 7 November, targets Firecracker. I read it with one question: could this happen in Koala? Every network packet carries a checksum. Computing it costs CPU, so virtio lets the guest hand that job to the host: “the checksum starts here, write it there.” That shortcut is an offload , and it’s on by default in most fast VM networking. The kernel fix landed upstream on 14 October 2026. The bug gets patched. The pattern stays. The attack needs guest packets to reach the host kernel’s network stack with the hints attached. TAP and vhost-net, the usual fast paths, do exactly that. Koala uses neither. A virtio device and the guest agree on features at boot. Koala’s network device offers only two that reach the guest: a MAC address and modern virtio. No offloads, so the guest can’t even send t

cae9095107acde39.summary: Vector databases rely on Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) indexes for similarity search, but a graph built from data alone can be poorly matched to a skewed or changing query workload. We present REWEAVE (Reward-Guided Rewiring of Vector Graphs), an online index-maintenance method that learns edge utility from query feedback and periodically rewires the bottom layer within the original per-node degree cap. The method supports sparse exact-neighbor feedback combined with self-labels, and standard HNSW serving without learning overhead once adaptation is disabled. Under explicit assumptions we prove value-estimation and graph-stabilization guarantees. Under stationary skew, REWEAVE improves held-out recall by up to 23.3 percentage points over HNSW. In comparisons with query-aware baselines on up to 100M vectors, it achieves up to 3.3x NGFix's query throughput at recall@100 of 0.80. On Amazon-ESCI with query drift, it increases stream recall@100 from 0.745 to 0.979 with 34% fewer search distance computations than frozen HNSW. These results illustrate the potential to improve retrieval quality and reduce search effort within an existing graph-degree budget, while incurring additional work during adaptation.

cd47cd6f74442984.content_excerpt: FlashStates: Unlocking Flexible Hybrid State Management for Agentic LLM Inference Chenxi Li 1,* , Weili Xu 2,*,† , Tianyi Zhang 1 , Jue Wang 1 , Zhongzhu Zhou 1 , Chenfeng Xu 3 1 Together AI 2 University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign 3 University of Texas at Austin FlashStates decouples recurrent checkpoint positions from KV-cache block boundaries, achieving fine-grained state reuse without dense checkpoint storage. In a hybrid model, attention keeps KV for every token, but each recurrent layer keeps one state that it overwrites as it reads. Resuming at a position needs the KV and a checkpoint taken exactly there; we call the pair a hybrid state. Each agent turn re-sends its whole context. Ideally, the engine computes only the tokens added since the previous turn ended. Any earlier token it computes again is redundant prefill , caused by one of three misses. Below 40 sessions, placement and dependency misses cause most of the redundant prefill in vLLM and SGLang. Capacity misses grow only from about 40 sessions. SGLang checkpoints every 256 tokens, so it has few placement misses (b). At 32 sessions, however, it keeps 4.2× as many checkpoints per request as vLLM. They compete for a fixed-size state pool, which causes its dependency misses (c). FlashStates saves recurrent checkpoints exactly where turns resume, and keeps or evicts each checkpoint together with the KV it depends on. ce9f8f3fe2d7cb93.summary: Hierarchical text embedding models offer variable-length representations, while quantization reduces numerical precision; both aim to improve computational efficiency. This work is an empirical benchmark study of how these two orthogonal, already-established techniques interact. We evaluate 38 tasks from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) using four transformer-based embedding models, covering 1D and 2D hierarchical representations combined with 32-bit, 8-bit, and binary quantization, for 168 configurations per task. We report each efficiency dimension separately: theoretical per-vector storage and end-to-end evaluation time. Under a Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc analysis, int8 quantization is statistically indistinguishable from float32 for pair classification and re-ranking and costs at most 1.5 percentage points overall, whereas binary quantization is significantly worse across every task category. Halving the embedding dimension once is not statistically detectable above $m=16$; two successive halvings always are. Combining an 8x dimensionality reduction with int8 yields a 32x reduction in per-vector storage at 94.4% of baseline effectiveness. Because evaluation times were measured once, we treat them as indicative: we find no evidence that quantization speeds up evaluation, whereas sampling from intermediate layers shortens it substantially. Retrieval degrades far faster than every other category, so we report findings per task category.

Because XAINs are bound to a ground-truth artefact, fairness concerns not only what a narrative says and how, but also whether it is equally faithful across social groups. We introduce fairness in XAINs as a new field of research and propose a framework that generates narratives under three conditions (protected attribute disclosed, withheld, or counterfactually swapped), allowing five comparisons that pinpoint the cause of disparities. We find significant disparities across all datasets, metric families and models, arising in two ways. cf14be16001b7e5c.summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly operate with shell access, allowing them to write scripts, move files, alter permissions, and modify system configurations. However, an agent may achieve a user's goal while causing unintended harm, such as deleting unrelated files, weakening access controls, or corrupting data, in response to benign inputs without explicit jailbreaking. This failure mode is particularly important because apparent task success may reassure users that an agent behaved correctly, causing harmful side effects to go unnoticed. We call this harmful success: the agent successfully completes the intended benign task while simultaneously causing unintended harm. Despite its importance, harmful success is difficult to measure because conventional task-success metrics overlook harmful behaviors, while existing safety evaluations are often designed solely to assess harmful outcomes. We introduce VeriHarm, an automatic framework for constructing programmatically verifiable benchmarks that directly measure harmful success. VeriHarm minimally perturbs coding tasks to elicit unintended harmful behavior while maintaining the benignity of the task and preserving the original task objective. It then synthesizes executable harm tests that, together with the original task-correctness tests, evaluate both task accuracy and harmful outcomes.
